The Iron Cage of Social Robotics | ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction

# The Iron Cage of Social Robotics

Author: Karolina Zawieska Authors Info & Claims

ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction, Volume 14, Issue 1

Article No.: 18, Pages 1 - 10

https://doi.org/10.1145/3695772

Published: 21 December 2024 Publication History

Contents

## Abstract

This article focuses on the conviction that has been popular within parts of the Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) community and beyond that social robots are or soon will become part of our everyday lives. Given the limited availability of social robots on the market and their evident absence in everyday environments, such a conviction is viewed here as highly inaccurate and, hence, quite astonishing in its prevalence and power. We argue that since social robots continue to be research platforms in the first place, depicting them as everyday objects leads to a profound paradox that hinders the successful integration of robots into society. A big part of the problem is in rigid conceptualisations of the social robot and conventional views of everyday life. In an attempt to offer an alternative approach, we propose to redefine the dominant perspectives on ‘interaction’ in HRI research to embrace the notion of ‘integration’ and ‘lived experience’ instead and by doing so, capture the complexity and transformative potential of the everyday. We argue that ‘everyday life’ can potentially become not so much a point of arrival as a point of departure for HRI research and a catalyst for critical and creative thinking of human-robot futures.

## 1 Where Are Social Robots?

Social robotics and Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) are fascinating research fields and occasionally a cause of professional surprise and wonder (given a significant overlap between the two [1– 4], these two fields are addressed together here). For example, in 2014, a large absence of sociology from research dedicated to social robots was found by one of the sociologists ‘quite astonishing’ [5, p. 108] (the situation that since then to some extent has improved [6– 11]). Others have been surprised by the prevalence of positive feelings people tend to express towards social robots [12] or described a new era coming for AI and ‘emotional’ robots as ‘amazing’ [13, p. 305]. What we now find equally astonishing is the existence of a strong conviction or belief (the two belong to the same family of meanings [14, p. 326] that social robots are certainly on the path of becoming part of our everyday lives [3, 6, 15– 17].

This is because despite the popularity of what we call here ‘the social robot project’ (the totality of resources and efforts dedicated to bringing social robots into society), social robots are obviously largely absent from our everyday physical and social environments. If we consider commercial availability of social robots as one of the key measures of their implementation into people’s everyday lives, so far, the success has been very limited, or ‘almost non-existent’ [18]. Instead, a recent survey on the design and evolution of social robots [19] has classified most of the social robots up to date as research prototypes, and only about 28.6% of them as commercially available. From a robotics industry point of view, humanoids (which can be seen as social robots) and robots that have been commercially deployed have sometimes been classified as two different categories that are not mutually inclusive [20]. Also, many social robotics start-ups and commercialisation initiatives have failed completely [18, 21, 22]. And yet, a discourse promoting social robots as everyday technologies, as well as a conviction that we are on the verge of ‘a robotics revolution,’ are surprisingly powerful and widespread in academia, industry and mass media [23– 30]. While the presence of such narratives in the public and business domains is at least to some extent ‘justified,’ we find it puzzling that they also manifest among at least some parts of the HRI community that specialises in the study of social robots and HRI.

Of course, not everyone is enthusiastic or optimistic about the possibility of bringing social robots into society. There has been a number of concerns raised regarding the potential consequences of the entire process, whether for the specific end-users’ groups or a society as a whole and with particular attention to people’s acceptance of robots in daily life [31– 35]. Whether robots can even serve as ‘technological fixes’ for fundamental societal challenges has also been questioned [24, 36], and the complexity of the everyday world that makes it a ‘wicked problem’ for robotics is acknowledged [37]. The fact that it is notoriously difficult to successfully scale up and adopt social robot solutions across the world keeps the entire social robot project and its enthusiasts in check. And yet, even these critical and more nuanced assessments of the prospect of living with (social) robots are often developed in relation to the assumption that the arrival of robotic technologies is largely inevitable. While it has sometimes been explicitly noted that this is not yet the case [35, 38, 39], claims according to which technologically optimistic views of the human-robot futures are not the only nor necessary development [24], human social interaction with robots is ‘a conceptual impossibility’ [40, p. 107], or the idea of having social robots in everyone’s home is ‘doomed’ [18] are rare. In other words, while it has sometimes been recognised that ‘robots have barely begun to enter human lives’ [38, p. 351], it is still often assumed that we have reached ‘the robotic moment’ [38, 41, 42] or ‘a tipping point’ [35] that sets us on a direct path to embrace social robots in daily lives.

There can be a number of reasons why the conviction about the (future) ubiquity of social robots is so popular, or at least taken for granted in HRI, from the overwhelming techno-scientific culture the HRI research is also part of the specificity of market and funding systems that constantly demand to innovate, to modern capitalist models that aim to maximise the number of customers and sales. One should also remember that the public discourse that promotes social robots as breakthrough inventions and an endeavour worth pursuing in research, industry and education does not necessarily correspond to the more sceptical views expressed by some of the HRI researchers in private). As discussed below, we argue here that at least part of the explanation may be in a lack of a systematic reflection on everyday life in HRI, and the underlying static concept of the human ‘everyday’ and related notions such as ‘sociality.’ This also translates into rather cautious definitions and goals set for social robotics, where neither robotics systems nor human engagement with social robots truly advances. Last but not least, we argue that while keeping in mind that the social robot project may actually never materialise, the key to overcoming the deadlock is in moving away from studying ‘interaction’ in HRI towards conceptualising human engagement with social robots in terms of ‘integration’ and ‘life worlds’.

## 2 Research Stagnation

It is interesting to observe that despite nearly three decades of research into social robotics, there is no universal definition of a social robot. Questions such as ‘What is a social robot?’ and ‘what makes a robot social?’ still dominate related research [4– 6, 18, 43– 47]. To this day, they often serve as the opening of research articles and conference presentations, and no one seems to question the need for it. Possible answers include attempts to identify essential features or metrics for social robots and related HRI to be considered ‘social’ [3, 19, 48, 49], as well as claims about what type of robots are ‘really’ social [5, 44], or what makes their design successful or ‘good’ [15, 19, 50]. Different explanations are largely dependent on one’s stance on whether robots can actually be social or only perceived as such [6, 44, 48, 51], or whether one aims to address ‘social’ or ‘sociable’ robots [52]. While initially these questions involved highly pioneering work [15, 44, 53], nowadays, the discussion often aims to clarify, systematize or improve the existing definitions of social robots [16, 19, 45], particularly as our knowledge about human engagement with social robots ‘in-the-wild’ expands and evolves. What different research definitions and approaches have in common is an emphasis on sociality and social interaction as a key goal and measures of success for social robots [19, 49, 54– 57].

In order to facilitate the implementation of social robots into real-world physical and social environments, the HRI field has become increasingly inclusive in terms of its scope and content (it is not a coincidence that the theme of the 2024 edition of the ACM/IEEE HRI conference was ‘HRI for all’ [58]), as well as disciplines and perspectives involved, to include for example feminist approaches [59, 60], philosophy [61– 64], arts [65– 67], as well as contributions from policy-makers [68]. Recent developments in HRI also include a growing attention and systematic study of contextual factors, socio-cultural dynamics and people’s involvement with robots [69, 70]. With thousands of academic papers published, hundreds of robotic platforms built, and numerous attempts made to bring social robots to market [16, 19], research and development in social robotics may seem to be thriving, to the point of being on the verge of a revolution indeed. And yet, the understanding of what is a social robot, and what makes it social has been largely the same for the last two decades. To this day, many articles (see e.g., [16, 19, 50, 71]) rely on the notions coined in the early 2000s [15, 51, 54, 72, 73]. In line with such definitions, social robots continue to be generally understood as robots ‘designed for social interaction with humans on human terms’ [52], and their key defining features remain more or less the same. Of course, there is nothing inherently wrong with referring to ‘old’ concepts, particularly in the case of such young fields as social robotics and HRI. Both fields still strive to develop and agree on their own theoretical and methodological canon, as well as ensure research rigour and reproducibility [4, 61, 74, 75]. This is in a situation where social robots are still ‘a puzzle’ [47], especially the nature of human engagement with social robots ‘in-the-wild’. What is striking, however, is that research on social robots continues to address what is known and what is possible rather than experiment with radically new ideas that one could expect from such a novel field as social robotics and HRI.

Part of the explanation may be simply in pragmatic choices and business calculations, where ‘social roboticists have made some simplifying choices that make successes more likely’ [76, p. 2116]. In line with such logic, most of the consumer social robots have been envisioned as servants, companions and carers to a varying degree [18], rather than in roles that would be entirely new to society. A similar trend applies to specific types of social robots: According to a recent study into the use of interactive robots in healthcare, ‘[m]ost of the robot applications… own some form of novelty, but the application areas are still traditional’ [77, p. 14]. Clearly, such choices are never made by individual researchers alone but rather emerge from an interplay of specific institutional settings, market demands, socio-cultural frameworks, ethical considerations and so on.
